docs.preview:
# Contributing

Hey! Thank you for deciding to contribute to Mock Service Worker! This page will help you land your first contribution by giving you a better understanding about the project's structure, dependencies, and development workflow.

## Tools

Getting yourself familiar with the tools below will substantially ease your contribution experience.

- [TypeScript](https://www.typescriptlang.org/)
- [Vitest](https://vitest.dev/)
- [Playwright](https://playwright.dev/)

## Dependencies

Mock Service Worker depends on multiple other libraries.

| Library name                                            | Purpose                                                                  |
| ------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| [cookies](https://github.com/mswjs/cookies)             | Enables cookies persistence and inference between environments.          |
| [headers-utils](https://github.com/mswjs/headers-utils) | `Headers` polyfill to manage request/response headers.                   |
| [interceptors](https://github.com/mswjs/interceptors)   | Provisions request interception in Node.js (internals of `setupServer`). |

There are cases when an issue originates from one of the said dependencies. Don't hesitate to address it in the respective repository, as they all are governed by the same team.

## Getting started

### Fork the repository

Please use the GitHub UI to [fork this repository](https://github.com/mswjs/msw) (_read more about [Forking a repository](https://docs.github.com/en/github/getting-started-with-github/fork-a-repo)_). Mock Service Worker has forked builds enabled in the CI, so you will see the build status of your fork's branch.

### Install

```bash
$ cd msw
$ pnpm install
$ pnpm start
```

> Please use [PNPM][pnpm-url] version 8.15 while working on this project.
> Guide on how to install a specific PNPM version can be [found here][pnpm-install-guide-url].

## Git workflow

```bash
# Checkout the default branch and ensure it's up-to-date
$ git checkout main
$ git pull --rebase

# Create a feature branch
$ git checkout -b feature/graphql-subscriptions

# Commit the changes
$ git add .
$ git commit
# Follow the interactive prompt to compose a commit message

# Push
$ git push -u origin feature/graphql-subscriptions
```

We are using [Conventional Commits](https://conventionalcommits.org/) naming convention. It helps us automate library releases and ensure clean and standardized commit tree. Please take a moment to read about the said convention before you name your commits.

> **Tip:** running `git commit` will open an interactive prompt in your terminal. Follow the prompt to compose a valid commit message.

Once you have pushed the changes to your remote feature branch, [create a pull request](https://github.com/open-draft/msw/compare) on GitHub. Undergo the process of code review, where the maintainers of the library will help you get the changes from good to great, and enjoy your implementation merged to the default branch.

> Please be respectful when requesting and going through the code review. Everyone on the team is interested in merging quality and well tested code, and we're hopeful that you have the same goal. It may take some time and iterations to get it right, and we will assist you throughout the process.

## Build

Build the library with the following command:

```bash
$ pnpm build
```

## Tests

### Testing levels

There are two levels of tests on the project:

- [Unit tests](#unit-tests), cover small independent functions.
- [Integration tests](#integration-tests), test in-browser usage scenarios.

**Always begin your implementation from tests**. When tackling an issue, a test for it must be missing, or is incomplete. When working on a feature, starting with a test allows you to model the feature's usage before diving into implementation.

### Unit tests

#### Writing a unit test

Unit tests are placed next to the tested code. For example, if you're testing a newly added `multiply` function, create a `multiply.test.ts` file next to where the function is located:

```bash
$ touch src/utils/multiply.test.ts
```

Proceed by writing a unit test that resembles the usage of the function. Make sure to cover all the scenarios

```ts
// src/utils/multiply.test.ts
import { multiply } from './multiply'

test('multiplies two given numbers', () => {
  expect(multiply(2, 3)).toEqual(6)
})
```

> Please [avoid nesting](https://kentcdodds.com/blog/avoid-nesting-when-youre-testing/) while you're testing.

#### Running a single unit test

Once your test is written, run it in isolation.

```bash
$ pnpm test:unit src/utils/multiply.test.ts
```

At this point, the actual implementation is not ready yet, so you can expect your test to fail. **That's perfect**. Add the necessary modules and logic, and gradually see your test cases pass.

#### Running all unit tests

```bash
$ pnpm test:unit
```

### Integration tests

We follow an example-driven testing paradigm, meaning that each integration test represents a _usage example_. Mock Service Worker can be used in different environments (browser, Node.js), making such usage examples different.

> **Make sure that you [build the library](#build) before running the integration tests**. It's a good idea to keep the build running (`pnpm start`) while working on the tests. Keeping both compiler and test runner in watch mode boosts your productivity.

#### Browser integration tests

You can find all the browser integration tests under `./test/browser`. Those tests are run with Playwright and usually consist of two parts:

- `[test-name].mocks.ts`, the usage example of MSW;
- `[test-name].test.ts`, the test suite that loads the usage example, does actions and performs assertions.

It's also a great idea to get familiar with our Playwright configuration and extensions:

- [**Playwright configuration file**](./test/browser/playwright.config.ts)
- [Playwright extensions](./test/browser/playwright.extend.ts)

Let's write an example integration test that asserts the interception of a GET request. First, start with the `*.mocks.ts` file:

```js
// test/browser/example.mocks.ts
import { http, HttpResponse } from 'msw'
import { setupWorker } from 'msw/browser'

const worker = setupWorker(
  http.get('/books', () => {
    return HttpResponse.json([
      {
        id: 'ea42ffcb-e729-4dd5-bfac-7a5b645cb1da',
        title: 'The Lord of the Rings',
        publishedAt: -486867600,
      },
    ])
  }),
)

worker.start()
```

> Notice how there's nothing test-specific in the example? The `example.mocks.ts` file is a copy-paste example of intercepting the `GET /books` request. This allows to share these mocks with the users as a legitimate example, because it is!

Once the `*.mocks.ts` file is written, proceed by creating a test file:

```ts
// test/browser/example.test.ts
import * as path from 'path'
import { test, expect } from './playwright.extend'

test('returns a mocked response', async ({ loadExample, fetch }) => {
  // Compile the given usage example on runtime.
  await loadExample(new URL('./example.mocks.ts', import.meta.url))

  // Perform the "GET /books" request in the browser.
  const res = await fetch('/books')

  // Assert the returned response body.
  expect(await res.json()).toEqual([
    {
      id: 'ea42ffcb-e729-4dd5-bfac-7a5b645cb1da',
      title: 'The Lord of the Rings',
      publishedAt: -486867600,
    },
  ])
})
```

##### Running all browser tests

Make sure Playwright chromium has been installed before running browser tests.

```sh
pnpm test:browser
```

#### Running a single browser test

```sh
pnpm test:browser ./test/browser/example.test.ts
```

#### Node.js integration test

Integration tests showcase a usage example in Node.js and are often placed next to the in-browser tests. Node.js integration tests reside in the `./test/node` directory.

Similar to the browser tests, these are going to contain a usage example and the assertions over it. However, for Node.js tests there is no need to create a separate `*.mocks.ts` file. Instead, keep the usage example in the test file dire

Mock Service Worker

The industry standard for API mocking in JavaScript.

Join our Discord server



## Features - **Seamless**. A dedicated layer of requests interception at your disposal. Keep your application's code and tests unaware of whether something is mocked or not. - **Deviation-free**. Request the same production resources and test the actual behavior of your app. Augment an existing API, or design it as you go when there is none. - **Familiar & Powerful**. Use [Express](https://github.com/expressjs/express)-like routing syntax to intercept requests. Use parameters, wildcards, and regular expressions to match requests, and respond with necessary status codes, headers, cookies, delays, or completely custom resolvers. --- > "_I found MSW and was thrilled that not only could I still see the mocked responses in my DevTools, but that the mocks didn't have to be written in a Service Worker and could instead live alongside the rest of my app. This made it silly easy to adopt. The fact that I can use it for testing as well makes MSW a huge productivity booster._" > > — [Kent C. Dodds](https://twitter.com/kentcdodds) ## Documentation This README will give you a brief overview of the library, but there's no better place to start with Mock Service Worker than its official documentation. - [Documentation](https://mswjs.io/docs) - [**Quick start**](https://mswjs.io/docs/quick-start) - [FAQ](https://mswjs.io/docs/faq) ## Examples - See the list of [**Usage examples**](https://github.com/mswjs/examples) ## Courses We've partnered with Egghead to bring you quality paid materials to learn the best practices of API mocking on the web. Please give them a shot! The royalties earned from them help sustain the project's development. Thank you. - 🚀 [**Mocking REST and GraphQL APIs with Mock Service Worker**](https://egghead.io/courses/mock-rest-and-graphql-apis-with-mock-service-worker-8d471ece?af=8mci9b) - 🔌 [Mocking (and testing) WebSocket APIs with Mock Service Worker](https://egghead.io/courses/mocking-websocket-apis-with-mock-service-worker-9933b7f5) ## Browser - [Learn more about using MSW in a browser](https://mswjs.io/docs/integrations/browser) - [`setupWorker` API](https://mswjs.io/docs/api/setup-worker) ### How does it work? In-browser usage is what sets Mock Service Worker apart from other tools. Utilizing the [Service Worker API](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Service_Worker_API), which can intercept requests for the purpose of caching, Mock Service Worker responds to intercepted requests with your mock definition on the network level. This way your application knows nothing about the mocking. **Take a look at this quick presentation on how Mock Service Worker functions in a browser:** [![What is Mock Service Worker?](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mswjs/msw/main/media/msw-video-thumbnail.jpg)](https://youtu.be/HcQCqboatZk) ### How is it different? - This library intercepts requests on the network level, which means _after_ they have been performed and "left" your application. As a result, the entirety of your code runs, giving you more confidence when mocking; - Imagine your application as a box. Every API mocking library out there opens your box and removes the part that does the request, placing a blackbox in its stead. Mock Service Worker leaves your box intact, 1-1 as it is in production. Instead, MSW lives in a separate box next to yours; - No more stubbing of `fetch`, `axios`, `react-query`, you-name-it; - You can reuse the same mock definition for the unit, integration, and E2E testing. Did we mention local development and debugging? Yep. All running against the same network description without the need for adapters or bloated configurations. ### Usage example ```js // 1. Import the library. import { http, HttpResponse } from 'msw' import { setupWorker } from 'msw/browser' // 2. Describe network behavior with request handlers. const worker = setupWorker( http.get('https://github.com/octocat', ({ request, params, cookies }) => { return HttpResponse.json( { message: 'Mocked response', }, { status: 202, statusText: 'Mocked status', }, ) }), ) // 3. Start mocking by starting the Service Worker. await worker.start() ``` Performing a `GET https://github.com/octocat` request in your application will result into a mocked response that you can inspect in your browser's "Network" tab: ![Chrome DevTools Network screenshot with the request mocked](https://github.com/mswjs/msw/blob/main/media/msw-quick-look-network.png?raw=true) > **Tip:** Did you know that although Service Worker runs in a separate thread, your request handlers execute entirely on the client? This way you can use the same languages, like TypeScript, third-party libraries, and internal logic to create the mocks you need. ## Node.js - [Learn more about using MSW in Node.js](https://mswjs.io/docs/integrations/node) - [`setupServer` API](https://mswjs.io/docs/api/setup-server) ### How does it work? There's no such thing as Service Workers in Node.js. Instead, MSW implements a [low-level interception algorithm](https://github.com/mswjs/interceptors) that can utilize the very same request handlers you have for the browser. This blends the boundary between environments, allowing you to focus on your network behaviors. ### How is it different? - Does not stub `fetch`, `axios`, etc. As a result, your tests know _nothing_ about mocking; - You can reuse the same request handlers for local development and debugging, as well as for testing. Truly a single source of truth for your network behavior across all environments and all tools. ### Usage example Here's an example of using Mock Service Worker while developing your Express server: ```js import express from 'express' import { http, HttpResponse } from 'msw' import { setupServer } from 'msw/node' const app = express() const server = setupServer() app.get( '/checkout/session', server.boundary((req, res) => { // Describe the network for this Express route. server.use( http.get( 'https://api.stripe.com/v1/checkout/sessions/:id', ({ params }) => { return HttpResponse.json({ id: params.id, mode: 'payment', status: 'open', }) }, ), ) // Continue with processing the checkout session. handleSession(req, res) }), ) ``` > This example showcases [`server.boundary()`](https://mswjs.io/docs/api/setup-server/boundary) to scope request interception to a particular closure, which is extremely handy! ## Sponsors Mock Service Worker is trusted by hundreds of thousands of engineers around the globe. It's used by companies like Google, Microsoft, Spotify, Amazon, Netflix, and countless others. Despite that, it remains a hobby project maintained in a spare time and has no opportunity to financially support even a single full-time contributor. **You can change that!** Consider [sponsoring the effort](https://github.com/sponsors/mswjs) behind one of the most innovative approaches around API mocking. Raise a topic of open source sponsorships with your boss and colleagues. Let's build sustainable open source together! ### Golden sponsors > Become our _golden sponsor_ and get featured right here, enjoying other perks like issue prioritization and a personal consulting session with us. > > **Learn more on our [GitHub Sponsors profile](https://github.com/sponsors/mswjs)**.

report.overview: MSW 3.0.1 is an ESM JavaScript library for describing mocked HTTP, GraphQL, WebSocket, and Server-Sent Events behavior during development and testing. Browser and Node setup APIs share a network-source, frame, and handler pipeline, while browser HTTP interception crosses a Service Worker message channel and Node interception uses @mswjs/interceptors. The inspected implementation also provides scoped Node handler overrides, persistent browser mock cookies, cross-runtime WebSocket clients, a worker-installation CLI, and Vite integration.
report.agent_prompt:
Onboard to msw at commit 6d6aef1640ace2ce2bd90252c71bdbc53262efd3. Treat this brief as a source-backed starting point, not an exhaustive inventory or proof of passing tests. The investigation inspected tests and CI without executing repository code. Preserve any active read-only restrictions: use rtk proxy for public-source reads and searches; do not install, build, test, browse, write files, access credentials, or publish unless the subsequent task permits those actions.

Read package.json, tsdown.config.ts, vitest.config.ts, test/README.md, and the relevant setup API first. This is an ESM package using pnpm 11.27.1 and requiring Node >=22.12.0. Conditional exports separate browser and Node entrypoints. GraphQL has its own subpath; do not assume older MSW import examples remain valid. CONTRIBUTING.md contains stale package-manager and test-directory guidance, so verify commands against current manifests and configuration.

The central architecture is defineNetwork → NetworkSource.queue → frame.getHandlers → frame.resolve. HandlersController groups request and websocket handlers, recursively registers sibling handlers, deduplicates references, and prepends runtime overrides. Browser setupWorker chooses ServiceWorkerSource or the Fetch/XMLHttpRequest fallback, and adds a separate WebSocket interceptor. Node setupServer uses ClientRequest, XMLHttpRequest, Fetch, and WebSocket interceptors plus AsyncHandlersController. server.boundary creates AsyncLocalStorage handler contexts; handler instances remain shared objects.

For HTTP changes, follow HttpNetworkFrame.resolve, executeHandlers, RequestHandler.run, and HttpHandler.parse/predicate. Lookup stops at the first returned response; matched handlers returning nothing fall through. Preserve once-handler rechecks, generator state, lazy finalize cleanup, request cloning, bypass markers, response cookies, and lifecycle events. Browser worker transport requires coordinated changes across mockServiceWorker.js, ServiceWorkerSource, WorkerChannel, and request deserialization. Stop must accommodate pending requests; worker compatibility checks warn instead of rejecting startup.

GraphQL links create query, mutation, operation, and subscription handlers. Subscription transports and WebSocket upgrades are sibling handlers. WebSocket links apply ordered extensions and maintain clients through IndexedDB or memory plus BroadcastChannel. SSE uses streamed HTTP responses and supports upstream forwarding. Vite provides virtual:msw, environment-specific network options, worker serving/emission, and serialized HMR teardown.

Before any permitted implementation, inspect adjacent unit tests and relevant integration/type tests, then propose a small diff. Avoid internal barrel imports; use concrete modules through the existing aliases. When execution is authorized, select the smallest package script and test file first, expanding to browser, Playwright, module, or typings checks only as relevant. Build-dependent tests import lib output. Never treat a listed test as a passing result, a source hypothesis as a confirmed vulnerability, or an automated release workflow as authorization to publish.

system_map.summary: The package exposes separate environment and protocol entrypoints around one shared network engine. Browser HTTP interception uses a Service Worker when available, with an interceptor fallback; WebSocket interception remains a separate source. Node combines four interceptor types and adds asynchronous handler contexts. Distribution consists of ESM modules, declarations, an IIFE bundle, and a generated worker asset, with release automation targeting npm.

claims.claim: package.json declares ESM, Node >=22.12.0, pnpm 11.27.1, and conditional exports that reject msw/browser in Node and msw/node in browsers.
The root entry exports HTTP, WebSocket, SSE, and utilities; GraphQL is exposed through its separate package subpath rather than the root barrel.
defineNetwork owns readyState, resolved options, the handler controller, and lifecycle event forwarding; each source queues frames that select handlers and resolve themselves.
setupWorker configures ServiceWorkerSource or FallbackHttpSource for HTTP and an InterceptorSource containing WebSocketInterceptor for WebSocket connections.
setupServer combines ClientRequest, XMLHttpRequest, Fetch, and WebSocket interceptors with AsyncHandlersController, then wraps the network in the common listen/close API.

Browser state includes a tough-cookie jar persisted under __msw-cookie-store__ and WebSocket client metadata stored in IndexedDB; Node leaves implicit cookie management to the client and uses memory when IndexedDB is unavailable.
tsdown builds ESM entries with declarations and source maps, a Node-platform Vite integration, and the MockServiceWorker IIFE; the worker build injects package version and checksum placeholders.

Scripts provide lint, build, Vitest projects, Playwright, module compatibility, typings, publint, and knip; scheduled/manual releases build and test before publishing through the provenance-enabled release profile.

feature_catalog.summary: Users describe network behavior through protocol factories and standard Request/Response objects. The public APIs support runtime overrides, lifecycle observation, explicit real-network traffic, and handler cleanup. GraphQL subscriptions and SSE provide imperative streaming controls, while WebSocket links expose clients and broadcast operations. CLI and Vite integration supply the browser worker through different installation paths.

claims.claim: http provides all, head, get, post, put, delete, patch, and options factories; HttpHandler accepts URL paths, regular expressions, or asynchronous predicates returning matches and optional params.
HttpResponse decorates standard responses for mock cookies and supplies text, JSON, XML, HTML, and ArrayBuffer helpers; text and JSON helpers calculate Content-Length unless supplied explicitly.
graphql.link(url) supplies endpoint-scoped query, mutation, operation, and subscription factories; selectors include names, RegExp, DocumentNode, typed document strings, and custom predicates.
GraphQL subscriptions expose publish, iterable-based from, error, complete, and passthrough controls; from publishes each yielded value without automatically completing the subscription.

ws.link exposes clients, connection listeners, broadcast, and broadcastExcept; optional ordered extensions transform the message domain and add APIs to connection events, while ws.onUpgrade is replaceable.
sse(path, resolver) matches GET requests accepting text/event-stream and supplies client send/error/close controls plus server.connect for forwarding an actual upstream stream.

Worker/server APIs expose events, use, resetHandlers, restoreHandlers, and listHandlers; Node adds boundary, while utilities provide bypass, passthrough, direct getResponse, and numeric/real/infinite delays.

msw init supports a destination, --cwd, --save, and saved worker directories; msw/vite provides auto or worker-only modes, virtual:msw, development worker serving, and conditional client-build worker emission.

data_flow.summary: Sources normalize intercepted traffic into protocol frames before shared resolution. HTTP handlers parse matching inputs and invoke resolvers in order, with handler state owning one-time and generator behavior. Browser response transport serializes across worker ports, whereas Node responds through interceptor controllers. Cookies and WebSocket client metadata have distinct persistence paths, and SSE sends encoded frames through a ReadableStream.

claims.claim: The worker serializes request metadata and an ArrayBuffer body, sends REQUEST with a transferred port/body, and the page reconstructs a FetchRequest before queuing a ServiceWorkerHttpNetworkFrame.

InterceptorSource receives request/controller pairs, stores HTTP frames in a WeakMap keyed by Request identity, and queues them; defineNetwork forwards frame events and supplies the current handler controller.
HttpHandler.parse gathers cookies and URL params or invokes a custom predicate; predicate combines URL matching with the HTTP method, and extendResolverArgs exposes params and cookies.
GraphQL input comes from GET query parameters, POST JSON, or multipart operations/map/files; parsing selects the requested document operation, and GraphQLHandler caches parsed results per Request.

executeHandlers awaits handlers sequentially and stops on a response; RequestHandler owns isUsed, generator iterator/results, and lazy finalize cleanup, including returning a thrown Response as the resolver result.

Browser mock responses cross the port as MOCK_RESPONSE using a transferable stream or buffered ArrayBuffer; the worker reconstructs Response, special-cases status zero, and buffers streamed navigation responses before committing navigation.

Mock response cookies are forwarded to document.cookie and stored against request.url before respondWith; later credentialed requests merge document cookies, jar cookies, and explicit Cookie headers, with headers taking precedence.

WebSocket storage persists only client id/url and reconstructs remote handles that send BroadcastChannel commands; SSE client.send instead serializes payloads into UTF-8 event frames enqueued on a response stream.

behavior_traces.summary: The following traces follow concrete startup, response, persistence, isolation, and reload paths through the inspected source. Browser startup waits for worker activation and a client confirmation before returning a registration. HTTP resolution distinguishes explicit bypass, unhandled traffic, fallthrough, and mocked responses. Node boundaries and browser persistence preserve different kinds of state, while Vite serializes network changes around hot updates.

claims.claim: Browser startup: setupWorker → start → ServiceWorkerSource.from → network.configure → network.enable → source.enable → #startWorker/getWorkerInstance → integrity check → activation wait → MOCK_ACTIVATE/MOCKING_ENABLED → return registration; unsupported Service Worker environments take FallbackHttpSource.

Browser mock request: worker fetch handler → handleRequest/getResponse → REQUEST → #handleRequest/deserializeRequest → queue → HttpNetworkFrame.resolve/executeHandlers → RequestHandler.run → respondWith/MOCK_RESPONSE → respondWithMock; RESPONSE subsequently drives page lifecycle events.

Unhandled HTTP flow: resolve emits request:start, checks bypass, calls executeHandlers, then executes onUnhandledFrame when no handler matches; unmatched CONNECT bypasses silently, and matched handlers returning nothing or passthrough bypass without the unhandled path.

Node startup/request flow: setupServer creates AsyncHandlersController and defineNetwork → listen configures onUnhandledFrame and enables sources → InterceptorSource.apply/listeners → #handleRequest/queue → frame resolution → controller.respondWith; close initiates network.disable synchronously.

Scoped override flow: server.boundary returns a wrapper → snapshots current handler buckets → AsyncLocalStorage.run creates a local context → use prepends per-kind overrides → frame lookup reads that context; outside a boundary, #getContext falls back to the server context.

Cookie persistence flow: storeResponseCookies extracts raw Set-Cookie → CookieStore.setCookie updates tough-cookie → persist serializes jar entries to localStorage; the next browser CookieStore constructor restores entries, and getAllRequestCookies includes them only for eligible credentials.

WebSocket flow: InterceptorSource queues a WebSocket frame → frame selects websocket handlers → handler.run matches and applies extensions → logger attaches → kConnect emits connection → link listener registers the client; broadcastExcept sends through local or remote client handles.

Vite flow: resolveId maps virtual:msw to runtime → virtual options select browser/server defaults → runtime defines a disabled network → user configure/enable starts mocking; beforeUpdate disables, afterUpdate resumes if previously enabled, and dispose retires the instance and removes HMR listeners.

testing_signals.summary: Tests and CI were inspected, not executed; their existence does not establish a passing result. Vitest separates unit, Node, browser, memory, typings, and CLI suites, while Playwright handles page lifecycle and multi-tab scenarios. Read assertions cover several important persistence, isolation, streaming, and teardown branches. This is a bounded inspection, and configured browser coverage is Chromium rather than evidence of cross-browser parity.

claims.claim: Vitest selects adjacent src unit tests and separate Node, memory, browser, types, and e2e projects; inspected configuration establishes suite routing, but no project was executed during this investigation.

Shared integration tests run in Node and browser unless filename suffixes exclude them; startNetwork creates the actual setupServer/setupWorker API, and its fixture defaults unhandled traffic to bypass unless options override it.

Concurrent boundary tests assert initial/override/initial responses in separate async scopes; browser cookie tests assert document forwarding, hidden Set-Cookie headers, multiple cookies, and continued cookie inference after localStorage quota failure.

Lifecycle assertions cover an in-flight mocked request surviving worker stop, later requests bypassing, finalize callbacks after abort including late registration, and simultaneous handler/source disposal rejection handling.

The Node frame-retention test warms up 500 failing requests, measures 1,500 more with forced GC and heap snapshots, and allows frame growth below 5% of the measured request count; this is a regression threshold, not a measured result from this brief.

Inspected protocol tests assert GraphQL subscription publication/completion, WebSocket extension decoding with unchanged upstream wire traffic, and SSE cessation of upstream reconnects after consumer close.

Vite tests build and inspect production output for removal of DEV-guarded mocks and then inspect rendered application behavior; CLI tests assert copied worker files and saved paths, while typings tests expect errors for incompatible declared response bodies.

CI specifies Node 22.23.2/24/26 with lint/build/Vitest/Playwright, compatibility jobs inspect package exports and TypeScript 5.9/6.0/7.0, and smoke automation tests external examples; browser configurations inspected here select Chromium, and no CI run status was retrieved.

risk_map.summary: These are source observations and explicitly marked hypotheses, not confirmed vulnerabilities. Network passthrough, persistent cookies, worker messaging, and serialized handler exceptions are the principal security-sensitive boundaries inspected. Shared lifecycle and streaming code has a broad behavioral impact, with regression tests documenting past failure modes. Documentation and automation also contain drift that should be verified before relying on their instructions.

claims.claim: Default warn handling permits real HTTP traffic after warning; explicit bypass and passthrough also reach the network, while unmatched CONNECT bypasses regardless of the configured unhandled strategy.

Browser mock cookies persist as JSON in origin localStorage and are also assigned to document.cookie; only persistence writes are caught for quota errors, while the initial localStorage.getItem call is outside that catch.

ServiceWorkerHttpNetworkFrame.errorWith converts handler exceptions into HTTP 500 JSON containing name, message, and stack; Node's interceptor frame instead throws ordinary errors, creating an environment-specific error surface.

WorkerChannel filters messages with a non-null source unequal to the selected worker, then accepts object payloads containing type; WebSocket managers process worker-stop window messages by type and remote BroadcastChannel commands by client id.

The worker checksum is a normalized-source MD5 compatibility marker: mismatch produces a warning and resolves the integrity promise instead of blocking startup. It should not be interpreted as an authentication or tamper-enforcement mechanism.
WebSocketHandler emits connection events synchronously, with an explicit FIXME about propagating asynchronous listener exceptions; the frame's try/catch surrounds that synchronous emission.

CLI destinations accept absolute paths or resolve relative paths without repository containment, then create directories and overwrite the worker file; saving replaces the msw object with workerDirectory, so unrelated msw fields are not preserved by that assignment.

Hypothesis: TypeScript-nightly may fail to exercise the intended RC check because compare writes step outputs without declaring job outputs, while test reads needs.compare.outputs and copies a version-specific config using a questionable shell interpolation. This needs workflow validation; no failure was observed.

extension_points.summary: The experimental API exposes the same source/frame abstractions used by the built-in environments. Handler factories, custom predicates, controllers, and sibling graphs provide additional composition boundaries. WebSocket extensions can change both runtime messages and inferred APIs. Storage implementations and Vite hooks are identifiable implementation seams, with public export/build configuration determining what consumers can import.

claims.claim: msw/experimental exports defineNetwork, NetworkSource, InterceptorSource, NetworkFrame, protocol frames, and handler controllers; a custom source implements enable and queues frames through an awaited emitter.

Custom NetworkFrame subclasses define protocol/data, handler selection, resolve, passthrough, errorWith, and unhandled diagnostics; resolve reports handled, unhandled, or skipped with true/false/null.

RequestHandler subclasses supply predicate/log and may override parse/extendResolverArgs; http's createHttpHandler factory constructs HttpHandler while custom HTTP predicates can calculate resolver params.

HandlersController abstracts getState/setState and supplies grouped use/reset/restore/dispose operations; AsyncHandlersController changes state ownership using AsyncLocalStorage rather than replacing request resolution.

attachSiblingHandlers composes hidden transport/upgrade handlers with a public owner; grouping recursively visits sibling graphs and deduplicates references, while listHandlers hides implementation siblings.

WebSocketExtension is publicly re-exported; ws.link accepts ordered extensions, handler.run invokes apply and extend, and ws.onUpgrade is read at request time so later overrides affect existing links.

onUnhandledFrame accepts an async callback receiving frame and defaults; predefined strategies suppress common HTTP assets, while custom callbacks must apply their own asset policy and defaults.error only prints.

WebSocketClientStore defines add/getAll/deleteMany with memory/IndexedDB implementations selected by the manager; new public utility modules are automatically discovered by tsdown and exposed through the ./utils/* export.

agent_handoff.summary: Start with current manifests and the shared network engine, then follow the affected environment and protocol boundary. Tests and CI were inspected, not executed; this brief provides no passing checks or exhaustive coverage assessment. Existing scripts and filename conventions identify focused checks for a later task that authorizes execution. Preserve worker protocol compatibility, handler ordering, cleanup semantics, and build/export boundaries when making small changes.

claims.claim: Use package.json and test/README.md as current workflow pointers: CONTRIBUTING.md recommends pnpm 8.15 and older test/browser paths, while the manifest pins pnpm 11.27.1 and current tests use protocol/API domains and filename suffixes.

Before request-resolution edits, read defineNetwork, HttpNetworkFrame, executeHandlers, and RequestHandler.run together; handler order, fallthrough, once rechecks, and response dispatch span those files.
Maintain strict TypeScript, kebab-case filenames, single quotes, and no semicolons; production source imports should target concrete modules instead of package barrels, as enforced by oxlint.

When execution is permitted, select the smallest relevant test:unit, test:node, test:browser, test:playwright, test:e2e, or test:ts script; inspected tests and CI remain unexecuted evidence in this report.

Build-dependent verification needs lib output: Vitest imports lib/vite/index.js and tsdown emits public entries/declarations; source export changes should be reviewed alongside package exports and module compatibility jobs.

Worker protocol edits require paired page/worker review plus checksum generation: copyServiceWorker injects placeholders, WorkerChannel translates payload to data, and browser response transport branches between streams and buffers.

Keep teardown synchronous at the source boundary even when handlers dispose asynchronously; worker stop intentionally retains channel handling for in-flight requests, and regression tests assert both pending-request completion and disposal rejection observation.

Review persistence and publication helpers without invoking them during source-only work: msw init writes destination files/package.json, the smoke script changes version and clones/installs examples, and release scripts publish externally.
